source_refs.note: Chapter 19 exercise (PDF 153-155, printed 149-151), solved: 10 MCQs with keys worked out from the chapter (no key printed), model answers to 8 short, 7 constructed and 6 comprehensive questions, and 6 numericals worked step by step.

blocks.prompt: 19.1 What is the half-life of a radio nuclide if 1/16 of its mass is present after 2h?
blocks.explanation:
1/16 = (1/2)⁴, so 4 half-lives have passed in 2 h = 120 min.
T½ = 120 min/4 = 30 min.

blocks.prompt: 19.2 Gamma radiations are emitted due to:
blocks.explanation: After α or β decay a nucleus is often left in an excited state; when it falls to a lower energy state it emits the energy as a γ-ray photon. So γ-rays come from the de-excitation of nuclei (de-excitation of atoms gives light or X-rays).

blocks.prompt: 19.3 Cadmium rods are used in nuclear reactor for:
blocks.explanation: Cadmium can absorb a large number of neutrons. Control rods of cadmium (or boron) are moved in or out of the core to cut down the neutrons available for fission and so control the chain reaction. Slowing neutrons is the moderator's job.

blocks.prompt: 19.4 The mass of fissionable material needed for self-sustaining chain reaction is called:
blocks.explanation: Critical mass is the mass of uranium in which one neutron, out of all the neutrons from one fission, produces further fission, so the chain reaction keeps going by itself. A smaller (sub-critical) mass cannot sustain it; a much larger (supercritical) mass gives an explosion.

blocks.prompt: 19.5 Graphite and heavy water are two common moderators used in a nuclear reactor. The function of the moderator is:

options.text: to slow down the neutrons to thermal energies
to absorb the neutrons and stop the chain reaction
to control the energy released in the reactor

blocks.explanation: Fission neutrons are very fast; slow (thermal) neutrons cause fission in U-235 much more easily. The moderator (water, heavy water, graphite) slows the neutrons down by collisions. Absorbing neutrons is the work of control rods; cooling is done by the coolant.

blocks.prompt: 19.6 The mass of a nucleus is always:

options.text: an integral number of proton masses
equal to the mass of all other nuclei of the same element
equal to the sum of the masses of proton and Neutron
less than the sum of masses of the constituent particles

blocks.explanation: The mass of a nucleus is always less than the total mass of its protons and neutrons. The missing mass is the mass defect Δm = [Zmₚ + (A − Z)mₙ] − m_nucleus (Eq. 19.1), which appears as the binding energy.

blocks.prompt: 19.7 Binding energy per nucleon is:
blocks.explanation: On the curve of binding energy per nucleon against A, the value is low for very light and very heavy nuclei and greatest (about 8.7 MeV, at iron-56) for medium nuclei, A about 50 to 80. These nuclei are the most stable.

blocks.prompt: 19.8 What remains unchanged in a fusion event?
blocks.explanation: In every nuclear reaction the total nucleon (mass) number and charge number stay the same. In fusion some mass is lost and changes into energy, so the mass and energy terms change, but the number of nucleons does not: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n has 5 nucleons on each side.

blocks.prompt: 19.9 Radioactive tracers are also employed to follow the path that various chemicals or food constituents take in:
blocks.explanation: Section 19.6: tracers follow chemical reactions in plants and animals, the uptake of fertilizer by plants and the movement of substances (digestion, blood flow) in the human body. So all of these.

blocks.prompt: 19.9 The K.E. of the fission fragments is ultimately converted to:
blocks.explanation: The fast fission fragments collide with the other atoms of the fuel; their kinetic energy is changed into heat. This heat makes steam which runs the turbine (section 19.3).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: This question is printed with the number 19.9 a second time; it is the tenth MCQ (19.10). The number is kept as printed.

blocks.prompt: 19.1 Define binding energy and how is it calculated?
blocks.explanation:
Binding energy is the work done on a nucleus to break it into its separate protons and neutrons (energy released when the nucleus is formed).
It is calculated from the mass defect:
Δm = [Zmₚ + (A − Z)mₙ] − m_nucleus
B.E = (Δm)c² (in joule; divide by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ to get eV). Example: for helium, B.E ≈ 27 MeV.

blocks.prompt: 19.2 Comment on the statement. “In radioactive decay, if the probability of decay per unit time is doubled, its half-life will also be doubled.”
blocks.explanation: The statement is wrong. The probability of decay per unit time is the decay constant λ, and T½ = 0.693/λ, so the half-life is inversely proportional to λ. If λ is doubled the half-life is halved, not doubled (the sample decays faster).

blocks.prompt: 19.3 After four half-lives, what percentage of a radioactive sample remains?
blocks.explanation:
After every half-life half of the nuclei remain: N = (1/2)ⁿ N₀.
For n = 4: N = (1/2)⁴ N₀ = N₀/16 = 0.0625 N₀
So 6.25 % of the sample remains (93.75 % has decayed).

blocks.prompt: 19.4 Why natural uranium is said to be low grade nuclear fuel? Describe briefly.
blocks.explanation: Natural uranium has only about 0.7 % uranium-235, the isotope that undergoes fission easily with slow neutrons; almost all the rest is uranium-238, which does not fission with slow neutrons but absorbs neutrons (and changes into plutonium-239). So natural uranium cannot easily keep up a chain reaction and gives little energy per kilogram; it is enriched to 2.4–3.0 % U-235 for reactors. Hence it is a low grade fuel.

blocks.prompt: 19.5 Give an application of a radioactive tracers in medicine.
blocks.explanation: Radioactive iodine (I-131) is used to check the thyroid gland. The patient takes a small dose; the thyroid absorbs it and a radiation detector measures how much is taken up. A diseased or hyperactive gland absorbs more than twice the normal amount. (I-131 is also used to treat thyroid cancer.)

blocks.prompt: 19.6 How is energy generated in the Sun? Describe briefly.
blocks.explanation: The Sun gets its energy by nuclear fusion in its core. At the very high temperature there (above 10 million °C) hydrogen nuclei move so fast that they overcome their electrostatic repulsion and fuse to form helium (thermonuclear reaction). In fusion some mass is lost and appears as energy, E = (Δm)c²: about 27 MeV for each helium nucleus formed. (In the Sun four protons join step by step into one helium nucleus, the proton–proton chain: beyond the chapter.)

blocks.prompt: 19.7 What is meant by the half-life of a radioactive material?
blocks.explanation: Half-life (T½) of a radioactive material is the time in which the activity (or the number of undecayed nuclei) of a sample falls to half of its starting value. T½ = 0.693/λ. Each element has its own half-life, e.g. radon 3.8 days, radium-226 1620 years, uranium-238 4.5 × 10⁹ years.

blocks.prompt: 19.8 What is meant by controlled and uncontrolled fission chain reaction? Describe briefly.
blocks.explanation: In a controlled chain reaction only one neutron (on average) from each fission causes a further fission, so energy is released at a steady rate (nuclear reactor). In an uncontrolled chain reaction more than one neutron from each fission causes further fissions, so the number of fissions grows very rapidly and a huge explosion results (atom bomb).

rows: On average one neutron from each fission causes another fission
More than one neutron from each fission causes further fissions
Rate of fission stays constant
Rate of fission grows very rapidly
Mass of uranium equal to the critical mass
Mass of uranium much greater than the critical mass
Extra neutrons absorbed by cadmium or boron control rods
No control on the neutrons
Energy released steadily; used in a nuclear reactor
Huge energy in a very short time; explosion (atom bomb)

blocks.prompt: 19.1 In what ways a nuclear power station is different to a fossil fuel burning power station called thermal power plant?
blocks.explanation: Both use heat to boil water into steam that runs a turbine and generator; they differ in how the heat is produced and in their fuel and waste.

rows: Heat from fission of uranium-235 (or plutonium-239) in the reactor core
Heat from burning coal, oil or gas in a furnace
About 200 MeV per fission; a small mass of fuel gives huge energy
A few eV per molecule burnt; huge amounts of fuel needed
Fuel loaded once runs the reactor for a few months
Fuel must be supplied continuously
Needs moderator, control rods, coolant and heat exchanger
Needs a furnace and boiler
No smoke or carbon dioxide; no air pollution
Gives smoke, CO₂ and other gases; air pollution and global warming
Radioactive waste with long half-lives; must be stored safely (old salt mines)
Ash and gases as waste; not radioactive
Radiation hazard; needs shielding and strict safety
No radiation hazard

blocks.prompt: 19.2 If fusion reactors are developed, what advantage are they likely to have over fission nuclear reactors?
blocks.explanation:
Likely advantages of fusion reactors over fission reactors:
1. More energy per nucleon: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n + 17.6 MeV, about 3.5 MeV per nucleon, against about 0.9 MeV per nucleon in uranium fission.
2. Plentiful, cheap fuel: deuterium (heavy hydrogen) is present in ordinary water (sea water); uranium is rare and must be enriched (beyond the chapter).
3. Clean product: the main product, helium, is not radioactive, so there is far less long-lived radioactive waste than from fission fragments.
4. Safer: there is no chain reaction that can run out of control; if conditions fail the reaction simply stops (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: 19.3 The activity of a radioactive sample is found to decay by 10 percent in a year. What will be the activity after another year? Explain.
blocks.explanation:
Radioactive decay is exponential (A = A₀e^(−λt)): in equal times the activity falls by the same fraction, not by the same amount.
After 1st year: A₁ = A₀ − 0.10A₀ = 0.90A₀
After another year: A₂ = 0.90A₁ = 0.90 × 0.90A₀ = 0.81A₀
So the activity will be 81 % of the original. In the second year it falls by 10 % of 0.90A₀, i.e. 9 % of the original activity, not by another 10 % of A₀ (it does not become 80 %).

blocks.prompt: 19.4 A source has an activity of 10 x 10⁴ Bq and a half-life of 20 minutes. What will be the activity of the source after one hour?
blocks.explanation:
Given: A₀ = 10 × 10⁴ Bq = 1.0 × 10⁵ Bq, T½ = 20 min, t = 1 h = 60 min
Number of half-lives: n = t/T½ = 60 min/20 min = 3
A = A₀(1/2)ⁿ = 1.0 × 10⁵ Bq × (1/2)³ = 1.0 × 10⁵/8
A = 1.25 × 10⁴ Bq
The activity after one hour is 1.25 × 10⁴ Bq (one-eighth of the start).

blocks.prompt: 19.5 What factors make a fusion reaction difficult to achieve?
blocks.explanation:
1. Both nuclei are positively charged, so they repel strongly (Coulomb force). Work must be done against this repulsion to bring them very close, so a very large energy is needed to start fusion.
2. The nuclei must move at very high speed: this needs a temperature of about 10 million °C (thermonuclear reaction). Such temperatures are ordinarily not possible; so far fusion has been produced only in the hydrogen bomb, triggered by an atom bomb.
3. No material container can hold matter at such temperatures; the hot plasma has to be held by strong magnetic fields (Tokamak, e.g. China's EAST) for long enough at high density.
4. Accelerators can make a few nuclei fuse (research) but cannot give continuous energy on a large scale. So fusion has not yet been controlled to produce electricity.

blocks.prompt: 19.6 In what way a nuclear reaction is different from chemical reaction? Explain.
blocks.explanation: A nuclear reaction changes the nucleus of an atom; a chemical reaction only rearranges the outer electrons (bonds) between atoms.

rows: Takes place in the nucleus (protons and neutrons)
Involves only the outer electrons of atoms
One element changes into another (transmutation)
Elements stay the same; atoms only rearrange into new molecules
Huge energy, millions of eV per reaction (about 200 MeV per fission)
Small energy, a few eV per reaction
Measurable mass changes into energy: E = (Δm)c²
Mass change is negligible
Mass number and charge number are conserved
Number of atoms of each element is conserved
Not affected by temperature, pressure or chemical combination (e.g. radioactive decay)
Rate depends on temperature, pressure, concentration and catalysts
Different isotopes of an element react differently
All isotopes of an element react alike

blocks.prompt: 19.7 Suggest a reason why neutron are absorbed in the boron rods and the rods become hot as a result of this reaction.
blocks.explanation: Boron (the isotope boron-10) has a very large ability to capture neutrons, especially slow neutrons, so boron rods (like cadmium) remove neutrons and control the chain reaction. A boron-10 nucleus that captures a neutron becomes unstable and breaks up: ¹⁰₅B + ¹₀n → ⁷₃Li + ⁴₂He + energy (about 2.8 MeV) (beyond the chapter). The fast lithium nucleus and α-particle collide with the atoms of the rod and their kinetic energy changes into heat, so the rods become hot and have to be cooled.

blocks.prompt: 19.1 Define the terms mass defect and binding energy. What information is given by the graphical curve between binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number?
blocks.explanation:
Mass defect: the mass of a nucleus is always less than the total mass of its protons and neutrons. The missing mass is the mass defect:
Δm = [Zmₚ + (A − Z)mₙ] − m_nucleus
Binding energy: the work done on a nucleus to break it into its constituent protons and neutrons. The missing mass appears as this energy (Einstein's mass-energy relation):
B.E = (Δm)c²
Example: for helium Δm = 0.048318 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and B.E ≈ 27 MeV. A better measure of stability is the binding energy per nucleon = B.E/A, the average energy needed to remove one nucleon.
Graph of binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number A (Fig. 19.1):
1. For hydrogen (one proton) it is zero; it rises steeply to helium (about 7 MeV), which shows a large energy release when hydrogen changes into helium.
2. It reaches a maximum of about 8.7 MeV at iron-56, the most stable nuclide; nuclei with A from about 50 to 80 are the most stable.
3. After that it decreases steadily to about 7.6 MeV for uranium.
Information given by the curve:
(i) Stability: the higher the binding energy per nucleon, the more stable the nucleus; very light and very heavy nuclei are less stable.
(ii) Fission: if a heavy nucleus (U-235, 7.6 MeV) splits into two middle nuclei (Ba, Kr, about 8.5 MeV), about 0.9 MeV per nucleon, i.e. about 200 MeV per fission, is released.
(iii) Fusion: if two light nuclei (e.g. ²₁H and ³₁H) join to form a heavier nucleus (A below about 50), energy is released.
(iv) In general, energy is obtained from any nuclear reaction in which the binding energy per nucleon of the products increases.

blocks.prompt: 19.2 What is nuclear fission? Explain critical mass and nuclear fission chain reaction.
blocks.explanation:
Nuclear fission: a reaction in which a heavy nucleus like uranium splits into two nuclei of roughly equal size, with the release of energy. Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found that slow neutrons split uranium-235:
²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3¹₀n + Q
About 200 MeV is released per fission. Reason: binding energy per nucleon is about 7.6 MeV for uranium and about 8.5 MeV for Ba and Kr, so 0.9 MeV × 235 ≈ 211 MeV is released. The fragments can differ (e.g. Sn + Mo, Xe + Sr); all are radioactive. U-235 and Pu-239 fission most easily with slow neutrons.
Fission chain reaction: each fission gives 2 or 3 neutrons. If these neutrons cause fission in more uranium nuclei, which give more neutrons, the reaction keeps itself going. This is a fission chain reaction. If it is not controlled, the number of fissions grows very rapidly and a huge amount of energy is released in a tiny time with an explosion (atom bomb).
Critical mass: in a thin sheet of uranium most neutrons escape and no chain reaction occurs; in a big enough lump most neutrons are absorbed before they escape. The mass of uranium in which one neutron, out of all the neutrons from one fission, produces further fission is called the critical mass (its volume is the critical volume).
1. Mass less than critical: the chain reaction dies out.
2. Mass equal to critical: the reaction proceeds at a steady rate (controlled chain reaction, nuclear reactor).
3. Mass much greater than critical: the reaction grows rapidly and explodes (atom bomb).
In a reactor, cadmium (or boron) control rods absorb the extra neutrons so that only one neutron per fission causes further fission.

blocks.prompt: 19.3 Describe a nuclear power reactor with its components and their functions.
blocks.explanation:
A nuclear reactor plays the same part in a nuclear power station as the furnace in a thermal power station: fission in the reactor produces heat, the heat makes steam, the steam runs the turbine and the turbine runs the generator.
Main parts and their functions:
1. Core and fuel: the fuel (uranium enriched to 2.4–3.0 % U-235; also plutonium-239 or uranium-233) is kept in cylindrical fuel rods in the core, where fission takes place and heat is produced (about 200 MeV per fission; core temperature about 500 °C).
2. Moderator: water, heavy water or graphite around the fuel rods. It slows down the fast fission neutrons, because slow neutrons cause fission in U-235 and Pu-239 much more easily.
3. Control rods: cadmium or boron rods that absorb neutrons. They are moved in or out of the core so that only one neutron per fission causes further fission, keeping the chain reaction steady. In an emergency or for repair they fall fully into the core and shut the reactor down.
4. Coolant and heat exchanger: water, heavy water or another liquid under high pressure carries the heat from the core to the heat exchanger, where it turns ordinary water into high-temperature steam (a pressurizer keeps the coolant under pressure).
5. Turbine and generator: the steam turns the turbine, which turns the generator to produce electricity.
6. Condenser: the steam leaving the turbine (about 300 °C) is cooled back into water using river or sea water and is pumped back.
In KANUPP heavy water was used as moderator and coolant and sea water to cool the steam. Used fuel is highly radioactive and is stored safely (e.g. deep in old dry salt mines). A thick concrete shield around the reactor stops radiation (beyond the chapter text).

blocks.prompt: 19.4 Describe why the very lighter nuclei and very heavy nuclei are unstable. How are they useful as a source of huge amount of energy?
blocks.explanation:
Why very light and very heavy nuclei are unstable: on the curve of binding energy per nucleon against A, the value is small for very light and very heavy nuclei and greatest (about 8.7 MeV) for middle nuclei (A about 50–80). A smaller binding energy per nucleon means the nucleons are less tightly bound, so these nuclei are less stable.
(i) Very light nuclei have few nucleons, so each nucleon is held by only a few neighbours (beyond the chapter: a large fraction of nucleons are at the surface).
(ii) Very heavy nuclei have many protons; their electrostatic repulsion acts across the whole nucleus while the attractive nuclear force acts only between near neighbours, so the binding per nucleon falls (beyond the chapter).
Use as a source of energy: energy is released in any nuclear reaction in which the binding energy per nucleon of the products increases; the extra binding energy comes from the mass lost, E = (Δm)c².
1. Fission of heavy nuclei: ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3¹₀n + Q. Binding energy per nucleon rises from 7.6 to 8.5 MeV, so about 0.9 × 235 ≈ 200 MeV is released per fission. Used in nuclear reactors (and the atom bomb).
2. Fusion of light nuclei: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n + 17.6 MeV. More energy per nucleon than fission. It needs about 10 million °C; it powers the Sun and stars (and the hydrogen bomb).

blocks.prompt: 19.5 What are radioactive tracers? Give some applications in medical diagnostics and treatment.
blocks.explanation:
Radioactive tracers: a radioactive isotope behaves chemically just like the stable isotope of the same element, but its location and amount can be found easily by detecting its radiation. A small amount of it, mixed with the stable element, acts as a tracer (indicator) to follow a chemical or biological process with a radiation detector.
Medical diagnostics:
1. Radio-iodine (I-131) is absorbed by the thyroid gland; the uptake shows whether the thyroid works properly (a diseased or hyperactive gland absorbs more than twice the normal amount).
2. Sodium-24 is used to study the circulation of blood (plasma volume).
3. Phosphorus collects in bones and cobalt in the liver, so they trace these organs; tracers also show the process of digestion and the movement of substances in the body.
4. Table 19.1: Fe-59 for iron in plasma, technetium-99m (6 hours) for thyroid uptake scans, I-131 for kidney tests, I-125 for plasma volume and vein flow.
5. Tracers in imaging devices (e.g. PET scanning) help to locate diseased tissue.
Treatment:
1. Large doses of I-131 are used against cancer of the thyroid gland.
2. Cancer cells multiply rapidly, absorb more radiation and are destroyed more easily than normal cells.
3. Radioisotopes in capsules (‘seeds’) are implanted in malignant tissue for local treatment.
4. Phosphorus-32 or strontium-90 is used for skin cancer.
The dose must be carefully controlled, because the radiation also damages healthy tissue.

blocks.prompt: 19.6 What is half-life? Derive the relation between number of half-lives and time. How we can, calculate the remaining and decayed quantity after several half-lives?
blocks.explanation:
Half-life (T½): the time in which the activity, or the number of undecayed nuclei, of a radioactive sample falls to half of its starting value.
Relation between number of half-lives and time:
If N₀ nuclei are present at the start,
after 1 half-life: N = N₀/2 = (1/2)¹N₀
after 2 half-lives: N = (1/2)(N₀/2) = (1/2)²N₀
after 3 half-lives: N = (1/2)³N₀
after n half-lives: N = (1/2)ⁿ N₀
If the time passed is t, the number of half-lives is n = t/T½, so
N = N₀(1/2)^(t/T½)
The same result comes from the decay law N = N₀e^(−λt): putting N = N₀/2 at t = T½ gives e^(λT½) = 2, λT½ = ln 2 = 0.693, so T½ = 0.693/λ.
Remaining quantity after n half-lives: N = N₀/2ⁿ
Decayed quantity after n half-lives: N₀ − N₀/2ⁿ = N₀(1 − 1/2ⁿ)
after 1st: N₀/2, after 2nd: 3N₀/4, after 3rd: 7N₀/8.
The same formulas hold for mass or activity. Example: 1000 atoms of polonium (T½ = 140 days) in 280 days: n = 2, remaining 1000/4 = 250, decayed 750.
Since half remains after each half-life, a radioactive sample never decays completely.

blocks.prompt:
19.1 Find the mass defect and binding energy of the deuterium. The mass of deuteron is 3.3435 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
(mass of proton mₚ = 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷, mass of neutron mₙ = 1.6749 × 10⁻²⁷) (Ans: 2.23 MeV)
blocks.explanation:
Given: m_d = 3.3435 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, mₚ = 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, mₙ = 1.6749 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (deuteron: Z = 1, A = 2)
Required: Δm and B.E
Mass defect:
Δm = (mₚ + mₙ) − m_d
Δm = (1.6726 + 1.6749) × 10⁻²⁷ kg − 3.3435 × 10⁻²⁷ kg
Δm = 3.3475 × 10⁻²⁷ kg − 3.3435 × 10⁻²⁷ kg
Δm = 0.0040 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 4.0 × 10⁻³⁰ kg
Binding energy:
B.E = (Δm)c² = (4.0 × 10⁻³⁰ kg)(3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)²
B.E = 3.6 × 10⁻¹³ J
B.E = 3.6 × 10⁻¹³ J/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ = 2.25 × 10⁶ eV
Answer: Δm = 4.0 × 10⁻³⁰ kg, B.E ≈ 2.25 MeV (≈ 2.2 MeV). The book's 2.23 MeV is the value from more exact masses; with the masses given to four decimals the result is 2.25 MeV.

blocks.prompt: 19.2 The decay constant of strontium is 1.99 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹. Find its half-life. (Ans: 9.7 hours)
blocks.explanation:
Given: λ = 1.99 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹
Required: T½
T½ = 0.693/λ
T½ = 0.693/1.99 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹
T½ = 3.48 × 10⁴ s
In hours: T½ = 3.48 × 10⁴ s/3600 s h⁻¹ = 9.67 h
Answer: T½ ≈ 9.7 hours (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt: 19.3 Half-life of krypton is 3.16 minutes. Out of 40 g of krypton, how much will be left after 12.64 minutes? (Ans: 2.5 g)
blocks.explanation:
Given: T½ = 3.16 min, N₀ = 40 g, t = 12.64 min
Required: mass left N
Number of half-lives: n = t/T½ = 12.64 min/3.16 min = 4
N = N₀(1/2)ⁿ
N = 40 g × (1/2)⁴ = 40 g/16
N = 2.5 g
Answer: 2.5 g of krypton is left (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt: 19.4 32 g sample of a radioactive material remain after 18 years. What is its half-life? (Ans: 3 years)
blocks.explanation:
Given: mass left N = 32 g, t = 18 years
Required: T½
The starting mass N₀ is not printed, so the question cannot be solved as printed (see the box). Method:
N = N₀(1/2)ⁿ, so 2ⁿ = N₀/N gives the number of half-lives n, and T½ = t/n.
The printed answer (3 years) means n = 18 years/3 years = 6 half-lives, so N = N₀/2⁶ = N₀/64. That needs a starting sample of N₀ = 32 g × 64 = 2048 g (about 2 kg):
2ⁿ = 2048 g/32 g = 64 = 2⁶, so n = 6
T½ = t/n = 18 years/6
T½ = 3 years
Answer: T½ = 3 years, if 1/64 of the sample (32 g out of 2048 g) remains after 18 years.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question does not print the starting mass of the sample, so the half-life cannot be found from it as printed. The printed answer, 3 years, fits only if 1/64 of the sample remains after 18 years (6 half-lives), e.g. 32 g left out of 2048 g.

blocks.prompt: 19.5 An alpha particle has an energy of 5.56 MeV when released from the radiam atom. Determine its velocity. (Ans: 1.68 × 10⁷ ms⁻¹)
blocks.explanation:
Given: K.E. = 5.56 MeV = 5.56 × 10⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 8.896 × 10⁻¹³ J
Mass of α-particle (⁴₂He nucleus, not printed): m ≈ 4 u = 4 × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg
Required: v
K.E. = ½mv², so v = √(2K.E./m)
v = √(2 × 8.896 × 10⁻¹³ J/6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)
v = √(2.68 × 10¹⁴ m² s⁻²)
v = 1.64 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹
Answer: v ≈ 1.64 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ (the book prints 1.68 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹; see the box). v is only about 5 % of c, so ½mv² may be used.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints 1.68 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. With K.E. = 5.56 MeV = 8.896 × 10⁻¹³ J and mα = 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, v = √(2K.E./m) = 1.64 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. The printed value would need a mass of about 6.3 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. The word “radiam” is printed for radium.

blocks.prompt:
19.6 Find the energy released during the nuclear reaction: ⁷₃Li + ¹₁H → 2⁴₂He
Mass of ⁴₂He = 4.00388u, ¹₁H = 1.00814 u and of ⁷₃Li = 7.01823u. (Ans: 19.2 MeV)
blocks.explanation:
Given: ⁷₃Li + ¹₁H → 2⁴₂He; m(Li) = 7.01823 u, m(H) = 1.00814 u, m(He) = 4.00388 u; 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg
Required: energy released Q
Mass before: 7.01823 u + 1.00814 u = 8.02637 u
Mass after: 2 × 4.00388 u = 8.00776 u
Δm = 8.02637 u − 8.00776 u = 0.01861 u
Δm = 0.01861 × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 3.09 × 10⁻²⁹ kg
Q = (Δm)c² = (3.09 × 10⁻²⁹ kg)(3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)² = 2.78 × 10⁻¹² J
Q = 2.78 × 10⁻¹² J/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J eV⁻¹ = 1.74 × 10⁷ eV
Answer: Q ≈ 17.4 MeV (with 1 u = 931.5 MeV: 0.01861 × 931.5 = 17.3 MeV). The book prints 19.2 MeV; see the box.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints 19.2 MeV. With the masses given, Δm = 8.02637 u − 8.00776 u = 0.01861 u, which is 17.3–17.4 MeV. The printed 19.2 MeV would need a mass defect of about 0.0206 u.
